To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the renal filtration of nanoparticles is a promising approach for the delivery of drugs and diagnostics, (ii) podocytes are an interesting target for the therapy of renal diseases, (iii) the renal filtration opens the door for the selective targeting of new cells like podocyte, which are not accessible by other delivery routes and (iv) the targeting can be performed via the αvβ integrin receptor.
Qdots are taken up into podocytes and that they can be specifically targeted to the αv-integrin receptor on podocytes.

(i) Qdots modified with the integrin binding peptide cyclo(RGD) show a specific binding to podocytes, (ii) Qdot uptake can be visualized in podocytes by confocal microscopy, and (iii) this approach opens the door for future therapy and diagnostic of podocyte-associated renal diseases.

the development of novel nanosystems for renal drug delivery and diagnostics.
the use of nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery and diagnostics.
the development of new nanomaterials for the diagnosis and therapy of diseases.

the results of this study are very promising for future therapeutic and diagnostic approaches of podocyte associated diseases.
the use of cyclo(RGD)-modified nanoparticles for targeting integrins is a promising approach to specifically target podocytes in vivo.

we were the first to show that nanoparticles can be targeted specifically to the renal podocytes after renal filtration.
the renal nanoparticle passage opens a new door for targeting cells like podocytes that are not accessible by conventional methods.

the renal clearance of nanoparticles opens the door for a specific targeting of podocytes and their integrin receptors, which are involved in the development of glomerular diseases like diabetic nephropathy.

nanoparticles are able to pass renal filtration and can be used for targeting specific cell types, such as podocytes.
